documents.title: Artificial Intelligence Policy
documents.summary: A short provost policy that sets a responsibility framework and leaves the decision on whether, when and how generative AI is used to each faculty member, who must state it in syllabi. Units may be stricter. It also points to CTL sample syllabus statements ranging from prohibition to unrestricted use.
documents.stance_why: The policy sets no ban or permission of its own: 'Faculty are responsible for deciding whether, when, and how generative AI is used in courses' and units may be 'more restrictive, not less restrictive'. Decision goes to instructors, so delegates.

units.why: The sentence defines generative AI as 'the ability of a machine to perform cognitive functions', which sets what the policy covers, so it is a definition (informs, general) typed P61 rather than the P56 framework.
units.anchor: the ability of a machine to perform cognitive functions associated with human minds

units.why: The purpose clause says the policy exists 'to provide guidance on the responsible use of generative AI', a statement of purpose for an institution-level framework, so P56 with informs modality.
units.anchor: provide guidance on the responsible use of generative AI
units.frag_start: The purpose of this policy is

units.why: The scope sentence says the policy 'applies to members of the Mercer community who are engaged in academic work and scholarship', defining who is bound; this is institution-level scope (P56), not a definition of AI (P61).
units.anchor: applies to members of the Mercer community who are engaged in academic work and scholarship

units.why: Units may adopt policies that are 'more restrictive, not less restrictive, than this University policy', which makes the university text a floor and lets units tighten; this is a scope rule of the framework (P56). P04 does not fit because the delegation is to units, not instructors per assignment.
units.anchor: more restrictive, not less restrictive, than this University policy

units.why: The policy requires that AI 'must be used responsibly and consistently with academic and professional codes of ethics', a general principle for all users, so P56 (principles) with must; the integrity link is a general standard, not a misconduct classification (P36).
units.anchor: must be used responsibly and consistently with academic and professional codes of ethics
units.frag_start: Generative AI must be used responsibly

units.why: 'Authors of content generated by AI are responsible for that content' makes the person who submits or publishes accountable for AI-generated content, which is P29 (own what you submit), addressed to all authors.
units.anchor: Authors of content generated by AI are responsible for that content.

units.why: 'Faculty are responsible for deciding whether, when, and how generative AI is used' places the decision with each faculty member, which is P04 (let each instructor set the rule).
units.anchor: Faculty are responsible for deciding whether, when, and how generative AI is used

units.why: 'Faculty must clearly communicate generative AI use to students in course syllabi, assignment instructions, and research guidelines' obliges instructors to state expectations in the syllabus, so P09.
units.anchor: Faculty must clearly communicate generative AI use to students in course syllabi

units.why: Students must understand and adhere to the faculty's communications 'in each of their courses', which binds students to the per-course rule set by instructors; P04 (instructor sets the rule) fits better than P29 because the duty is to follow the instructor's rule, and 'each of their courses' also shows course-by-course scope.
units.anchor: Students are responsible for understanding and adhering to faculty communications

units.why: The CTL 'provides example syllabus statements on generative AI for faculty consideration, ranging from strictly prohibited use of AI to unrestricted use of AI', which is support for faculty setting policy (P63) rather than a tier definition itself (P05).
units.anchor: provides example syllabus statements on generative AI for faculty consideration
units.frag_start: The Center for Teaching and Learning provides

documents.title: Guidance for AI Use in Teaching & Learning
documents.summary: Teaching-center guidance restating the provost policy and offering two frameworks for instructors to use: a three-color Traffic Light Framework and the five-level AI Assessment Scale. Each level is described briefly, from no AI to full AI.
documents.stance_why: The page repeats that 'faculty are responsible for deciding whether, when, and how generative AI is used' and supplies tiers (Green, Yellow, Red; No AI to Full AI) for instructors to pick from, so it sets no single stance and delegates with tiers.

units.why: Restates that 'faculty are responsible for deciding whether, when, and how generative AI is used in courses', handing the decision to instructors; P04.
units.anchor: faculty are responsible for deciding whether, when, and how generative AI is used

units.why: Says students are 'responsible for understanding and adhering to faculty communications' in each course, binding students to the instructor's rule; P04 as in the policy, since it follows the per-instructor rule.
units.anchor: students are responsible for understanding and adhering to faculty communications

units.why: 'Faculty must clearly communicate generative AI use to students in course syllabi, assignment instructions' obliges a syllabus statement; P09.
units.anchor: Faculty must clearly communicate generative AI use to students in course syllabi

units.why: 'authors of content generated by AI are responsible for that content' puts accountability on whoever submits AI-generated content; P29.
units.anchor: authors of content generated by AI are responsible for that content

units.why: 'Any use of AI must uphold academic integrity and compliance with university policies' with named policies (Academic Integrity, Data Security, IT Access and Use) is a general framework principle (P56), not a specific misconduct rule (P36).
units.anchor: Any use of AI must uphold academic integrity and compliance with university policies

units.why: The Traffic Light Framework is 'a practical way of categorizing AI use permissions in course syllabi and assignments', i.e. named colored levels; P05.
units.anchor: a practical way of categorizing AI use permissions in course syllabi and assignments

units.why: Green Light: 'Students are freely permitted to use AI tools in their course work or research', the open end of the tiers; P02 (permit by default for that tier) is the best fit, tier naming is covered in the previous unit.
units.anchor: Students are freely permitted to use AI tools in their course work or research.

units.why: Green Light says 'All AI-generated content must be cited', a citation duty on every AI output; P24.
units.anchor: All AI-generated content must be cited
units.policy: Under the Green Light tier, all AI-generated content must be cited.

units.why: Green Light says AI accuracy 'should be carefully evaluated by the user', a verification duty (P31) with should modality.
units.anchor: its accuracy should be carefully evaluated by the user

units.why: 'The course syllabus and assignment instructions provide a clear statement of permission' means the tier must be written down in the syllabus and assignment; P09.
units.anchor: The course syllabus and assignment instructions provide a clear statement of permission.

units.why: Yellow Light: 'Students may use AI tools with limitations' defines a middle tier of conditional use, typed P05 as a tier rather than a specific permitted use.
units.anchor: Students may use AI tools with limitations.

units.why: Yellow Light: 'Students are advised to consult with their professor about the appropriateness of AI for specific course tasks', i.e. ask when unsure; P10.
units.anchor: Students are advised to consult with their professor about the appropriateness of AI

units.why: Red Light: 'AI tools are not permitted. All student work must be completed independently', a ban on the work the syllabus governs; P01.
units.anchor: All student work must be completed independently, without the assistance of AI tools.

units.why: 'Unauthorized use of AI tools is considered a violation of the Academic Integrity Policy' classifies unauthorized AI use as misconduct; P36.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of AI tools is considered a violation of the Academic Integrity Policy.

units.why: The AI Assessment Scale is offered as 'guidance for assignments and assessments using AI' and a framework for communicating expectations; it names levels so P05.
units.anchor: provides guidance for assignments and assessments using AI
units.frag_end: communicating AI use expectations in courses.

units.why: 'No AI': assessment 'completed entirely without AI assistance in a controlled environment' is a no-AI level for assessments; P22 fits the controlled-environment wording, though the level also appears in the scale (P05) which the previous unit covers.
units.anchor: completed entirely without AI assistance in a controlled environment

units.why: 'AI Planning': 'AI may be used for pre-task activities such as brainstorming, outlining, and initial research'; brainstorming and ideation, P15.
units.anchor: AI may be used for pre-task activities such as brainstorming, outlining, and initial research.

units.why: AI Planning adds that 'assessments should emphasize the ability to develop and refine these ideas independently', a design instruction for assessments; P35.
units.anchor: assessments should emphasize the ability to develop and refine these ideas independently

units.why: 'AI Collaboration': 'AI may be used to help complete the task, including idea generation, drafting, feedback, and refinement' allows broad help including drafting; P16 is closest as it allows AI-produced work under the condition that students modify it.
units.anchor: AI may be used to help complete the task, including idea generation, drafting, feedback
units.frag_start: AI may be used to help

units.why: 'Students should critically evaluate and modify the AI suggested outputs, demonstrating their understanding' asks students to verify and own outputs; P31 over P30 because the focus is critical evaluation of output.
units.anchor: Students should critically evaluate and modify the AI suggested outputs, demonstrating their understanding.

units.why: 'AI Exploration': 'Students and educators co-design assessments to explore unique AI applications' redesigns assessment around AI; P35.
units.anchor: Students and educators co-design assessments to explore unique AI applications
units.frag_start: AI is used creatively to enhance

units.why: 'Full AI': 'AI may be used to complete any elements of the task' places no limit on AI use at that level; P16 (freely allowed generated work).
units.anchor: AI may be used to complete any elements of the task
units.frag_start: AI may be used to complete

units.why: Full AI level: assessments 'may also require engagement with AI', so AI use can be built into the work; P02 with unit_stance require.
units.anchor: Assessments at this level may also require engagement with AI

documents.title: Sample Syllabus and Assignment Guidance for AI Use
documents.summary: A detailed faculty guide with a recommended course baseline, Red/Yellow/Green assignment templates, disclosure and citation language, privacy and access rules, and guidance on detectors and evidence. It frames AI rules around protecting the learning each assignment measures.
documents.stance_why: It says 'Mercer faculty are responsible for deciding whether, when, and how generative AI may be used' and provides Red, Yellow and Green templates to adapt, so it hands the choice to instructors and lists tiers; its sample baseline prohibits AI unless an assignment permits, but that is a template.

units.why: 'AI should strengthen learning, not replace it' is a principle that AI must not replace student thinking; P32.

units.anchor: Human judgment remains accountable.

units.why: 'identify the knowledge, reasoning, practice, or performance the course and its assignments are intended to develop' tells instructors to ground any AI rule in learning goals before writing it; this is a policy-design step, nearest to P09 (what a statement must cover) though it also expresses the learning rationale (P41).
